bullets.treat: Support bleeding and infections, then consider transplant.
bullets.trap: Do not call this ordinary eczema.

source.recommendation: Wiskott-Aldrich is X-linked: thrombocytopenia, eczema, and combined immune defects.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The cytoskeleton protein in blood cells is missing.

front: A child begins to stagger, has dilated vessels in the eyes, and a high AFP. IgA is low.
bottom: The DNA-repair kinase is missing.

bullets.clue: Broken DNA is not fixed, so lymphoma risk is high.
bullets.treat: Support the ataxia, then avoid extra radiation.
bullets.trap: Do not treat the vessels as a primary eye infection.

source.recommendation: Ataxia-telangiectasia is ATM dysfunction: ataxia, telangiectasias, high AFP, and IgA deficiency.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The DNA-repair kinase is missing.

front: A boy has no T cells and no NK cells. B cells are present but do not work. The common cytokine receptor chain is gone.
bottom: This is the X-linked combined immunodeficiency.

bullets.clue: The common gamma chain is shared by several interleukin receptors.
bullets.treat: Transplant, then do not give live vaccines.
bullets.trap: Do not call it antibody deficiency alone.

source.recommendation: X-linked SCID is common-gamma-chain deficiency: absent T and NK cells, with nonfunctional B cells.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. This is the X-linked combined immunodeficiency.

front: The most common primary antibody gap. Sinus and gut infections, and anaphylaxis when given blood products.
bottom: IgA is missing.

bullets.clue: Transfused IgA can be the antigen that triggers anaphylaxis.
bullets.treat: Use washed cells if transfusion is required, then do not give intramuscular immunoglobulin casually.
bullets.trap: Do not call every low vaccine titer this disease.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: selective IgA deficiency
source.recommendation: Selective IgA deficiency can cause anaphylaxis to blood products that contain IgA.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. IgA is missing.

front: Dark urine on waking, a clot in an unusual vein, and red cells that lack two surface brakes on complement.
bottom: The GPI anchor is missing.

bullets.clue: CD55 and CD59 never attach, so complement punches the red cell.
bullets.treat: Anticoagulate the clot, then a complement blocker needs meningococcal vaccines first.
bullets.trap: Do not give iron alone and stop.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
source.recommendation: PNH is an acquired PIGA mutation. CD55 and CD59 are lost. Thrombosis is the leading threat.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The GPI anchor is missing.

front: Anemia, a high iron, and ringed sideroblasts. The X-linked enzyme needs vitamin B6.
bottom: ALA synthase in the red cell is weak.

bullets.clue: Iron is trapped in mitochondria around the nucleus.
bullets.treat: Give pyridoxine when the enzyme can respond, then remove the drug cause if there is one.
bullets.trap: Do not treat this as iron deficiency. Iron is already high.

source.recommendation: Sideroblastic anemia shows ringed sideroblasts and iron overload. X-linked ALA synthase needs B6.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. ALA synthase in the red cell is weak.

front: Severe anemia after the first months, a crew-cut skull, and hemoglobin made of mostly fetal chains. The genes have point changes, not deletions.
bottom: Beta chains are not being made.

bullets.clue: Four-gene alpha deletion is fatal before birth. Beta disease appears when fetal hemoglobin falls.
bullets.treat: Transfuse and chelate, then consider a curative transplant.
bullets.trap: Do not call every microcytic anemia iron deficiency.

source.recommendation: Beta-thalassemia major presents after the hemoglobin switch, with chipmunk facies and iron overload from transfusion.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Beta chains are not being made.

front: Fatal hydrops before birth. All four alpha genes are gone. The hemoglobin is tetramers of gamma chains.
bottom: No alpha chain was made.

bullets.clue: Three missing alpha genes cause a milder tetramer of beta chains after birth.
bullets.treat: This four-gene loss is not compatible with life, then genetic counseling is the point.
bullets.trap: Do not expect this child to present as a toddler.

source.recommendation: Deletion of all four alpha-globin genes causes hemoglobin Barts and hydrops fetalis.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. No alpha chain was made.

front: A young adult has bleeding and low platelets after a myeloid leukemia. The translocation fuses a retinoic-acid receptor.
bottom: Give all-trans retinoic acid.

bullets.clue: The cells are stuck as promyelocytes. The drug pushes them to mature.
bullets.treat: Start the differentiating drug, then watch for the differentiation syndrome.
bullets.trap: Do not wait for the clot studies. This leukemia consumes clotting factors.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: acute promyelocytic leukemia
source.recommendation: APL is t(15;17), RARA fusion. All-trans retinoic acid is started immediately because of DIC risk.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Give all-trans retinoic acid.

front: A jaw mass in a child, a starry-sky biopsy, and a translocation that puts a growth gene next to an antibody promoter.
bottom: c-myc is driven by the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus.

bullets.clue: The translocation is 8 and 14.
bullets.treat: Treat as a fast lymphoma, then protect against tumor lysis.
bullets.trap: Do not call every jaw mass an infection.

source.recommendation: Burkitt lymphoma is t(8;14), c-myc beside the immunoglobulin heavy-chain promoter. Tumor lysis risk is high.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. c-myc is driven by the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus.

front: A slow lymphoma. The translocation stops a death protein from being made.
bottom: BCL2 is overproduced.

bullets.clue: Chromosomes 14 and 18. The cells do not die on schedule.
bullets.treat: Name the death protein, then do not treat it like the fast starry-sky lymphoma.
bullets.trap: Do not use the same translocation for every B-cell lymphoma.

source.recommendation: Follicular lymphoma is t(14;18) with BCL2 overexpression, which blocks apoptosis.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. BCL2 is overproduced.

front: A lymphoma of older adults that behaves aggressively. The translocation raises cyclin D.
bottom: Cyclin D1 is overproduced.

bullets.clue: Chromosomes 11 and 14.
bullets.treat: Name cyclin D, then treat it as aggressive, not as the slow death-protein lymphoma.
bullets.trap: Do not swap 11;14 with 14;18.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: mantle cell lymphoma
source.recommendation: Mantle cell lymphoma is t(11;14) with cyclin D1 overexpression.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Cyclin D1 is overproduced.

front: A young adult has a node, night sweats, and large cells that mark CD15 and CD30. Spread is to the next node, not widely at the start.
bottom: Those two markers name the cell.

bullets.clue: Contiguous node spread is the pattern.
bullets.treat: Stage by the contiguous nodes, then treat. A noncontiguous jump is a different lymphoma.
bullets.trap: Do not call every large lymphoid cell this disease.

source.recommendation: Reed-Sternberg cells are CD15 and CD30 positive. Hodgkin lymphoma spreads contiguously.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Those two markers name the cell.

front: An older adult has a huge spleen, a dry tap, and cells with hairlike projections.
bottom: A BRAF change drives it.

bullets.clue: The marrow is fibrotic, so the aspirate is dry.
bullets.treat: A BRAF inhibitor is the modern path for many patients, then do not call it chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
bullets.trap: Do not expect smudge cells.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: hairy cell leukemia
source.recommendation: Hairy cell leukemia shows a dry tap, hairy B cells, and often a BRAF V600E mutation.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. A BRAF change drives it.

front: Bone pain, high calcium, kidney injury, anemia, and punched-out films. A different patient has a small antibody spike and none of those.
bottom: End-organ damage vs a quiet spike.

bullets.clue: The quiet spike is observed. The damage is treated.
bullets.treat: Treat the disease that has calcium, kidney, anemia, or bone lesions, then observe the quiet spike.
bullets.trap: Do not start chemotherapy for every antibody spike.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: myeloma vs MGUS
source.recommendation: Myeloma is a plasma-cell disease with CRAB features. MGUS is a small spike without those features.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. End-organ damage vs a quiet spike.

front: An older adult has blurry vision, a nosebleed, and a very high IgM. Bones are intact.
bottom: The blood is too thick.

bullets.clue: IgM is the large antibody that raises viscosity. Lytic bone disease is the other plasma-cell illness.
bullets.treat: Plasmapheresis for the viscosity, then treat the clone.
bullets.trap: Do not look for punched-out bones as the required finding.

source.recommendation: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia produces IgM and hyperviscosity without the lytic bones of myeloma.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The blood is too thick.

front: Rods in the myeloid blasts of an adult. A child is more likely to have lymphoid blasts.
bottom: Rods mean myeloid blasts.

bullets.clue: Lymphoid blasts in a child do not make those rods.
bullets.treat: Name the lineage from the rod, then start the matching induction.
bullets.trap: Do not treat every blast crisis as lymphoid.

source.recommendation: Auer rods are crystalline myeloid granules and indicate acute myeloid leukemia, classically APL when numerous.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Rods mean myeloid blasts.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A drug blocks new clotting factors and also the short-lived anticoagulant proteins. The patient clots before the blood thins.
bottom: The anticoagulant proteins fall first.

bullets.clue: Protein C and S have short half-lives, so a few doses create a clot window.
bullets.treat: Bridge with a fast anticoagulant, then continue the oral drug alone once the INR is stable.
bullets.trap: Do not start this drug alone in an acute clot.

source.recommendation: Warfarin depletes protein C and S before the pro-clotting factors, so heparin bridge is used at the start.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The anticoagulant proteins fall first.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A drug speeds antithrombin and is followed with the PTT. A different drug is followed with the INR.
bottom: Heparin vs warfarin monitoring.

bullets.clue: Heparin is the PTT drug. Warfarin is the INR drug.
bullets.treat: Stop heparin if the platelets crash on day 7, then use a non-heparin anticoagulant.
bullets.trap: Do not follow heparin with an INR.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: heparin vs warfarin monitoring
source.recommendation: Unfractionated heparin potentiates antithrombin and is monitored with PTT. Warfarin is monitored with INR.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Heparin vs warfarin monitoring.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A clot-busting drug can act only where fibrin is already present.
bottom: It activates plasminogen on the clot.

bullets.clue: Free plasminogen in the blood is not the target.
bullets.treat: Use it for a fresh clot in the right time window, then do not give it if there is bleeding or a dissection.
bullets.trap: Do not use it as a blood thinner for a stable patient.

source.recommendation: Alteplase activates fibrin-bound plasminogen. It is not an anticoagulant for chronic prevention.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. It activates plasminogen on the clot.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: One antiplatelet drug blocks ADP at P2Y12. Another blocks the fibrinogen receptor.
bottom: ADP receptor vs the final platelet receptor.

bullets.clue: The fibrinogen receptor is the last common step of platelet clumping.
bullets.treat: Hold the ADP drug for the labeled window around surgery, then do not stop aspirin in the early weeks after a stent.
bullets.trap: Do not treat them as the same pill.

source.recommendation: Clopidogrel blocks P2Y12. GPIIb/IIIa blockers stop fibrinogen binding, the final platelet step.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. ADP receptor vs the final platelet receptor.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A folate mimic is rescued by folinic acid. A different drug is made stronger by the same rescue molecule.
bottom: Rescue vs potentiation.

bullets.clue: The folate mimic is rescued in normal cells. The pyrimidine drug is potentiated.
bullets.treat: Give the rescue after the folate mimic, then do not give it to undo the pyrimidine drug.
bullets.trap: Do not swap the two.

source.recommendation: Leucovorin rescues methotrexate toxicity and potentiates 5-fluorouracil.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Rescue vs potentiation.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A gout drug blocks the enzyme that clears a leukemia drug. The leukemia drug level soars.
bottom: Xanthine oxidase clears both.

bullets.clue: The interaction is the point, not the gout.
bullets.treat: Cut the leukemia drug sharply if the gout drug must be used, then prefer a different gout drug.
bullets.trap: Do not combine full doses.

source.recommendation: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which metabolizes 6-mercaptopurine. The combination causes severe toxicity.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Xanthine oxidase clears both.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A cancer drug causes hemorrhagic cystitis. A protective drug binds the toxic metabolite in the urine.
bottom: Give the bladder protector with the drug.

bullets.clue: The toxic metabolite is acrolein.
bullets.treat: Hydrate and give the protector, then do not skip it because the urine looks clear today.
bullets.trap: Do not treat the bleeding with a platelet transfusion alone.

source.recommendation: Cyclophosphamide causes hemorrhagic cystitis via acrolein. Mesna binds acrolein in the urine.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Give the bladder protector with the drug.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A cancer drug scars the lung and spares the marrow.
bottom: The lung is the limit.

bullets.clue: Marrow suppression is not this drug's signature.
bullets.treat: Stop the drug for new cough or fibrosis, then do not push the dose because the blood counts look fine.
bullets.trap: Do not confuse it with the heart-toxic anthracycline.

source.recommendation: Bleomycin toxicity is pulmonary fibrosis. Myelosuppression is minimal.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The lung is the limit.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A red cancer drug dilates the heart. A chelator can be given to protect it.
bottom: The heart is the limit.

bullets.clue: The protective chelator does not treat an already failed heart by itself.
bullets.treat: Track the ejection fraction, then stop for a meaningful drop.
bullets.trap: Do not keep dosing through a falling ejection fraction.

source.recommendation: Doxorubicin causes dilated cardiomyopathy. Dexrazoxane is the cardioprotective chelator.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The heart is the limit.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: One vinca alkaloid numbs the fingers. Its cousin empties the marrow.
bottom: Neuropathy vs marrow.

bullets.clue: The neuropathy drug is the one used when marrow must be spared.
bullets.treat: Stop the neuropathy drug for severe numbness, then do not swap the toxicities.
bullets.trap: Do not give the neuropathy drug into the spinal fluid.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: vincristine vs vinblastine
source.recommendation: Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy. Vinblastine causes bone-marrow suppression.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Neuropathy vs marrow.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A platinum drug deafens and injures the kidney. A chloride diuresis lowers the kidney hit.
bottom: Protect the kidney with chloride diuresis.

bullets.clue: Hearing loss can be permanent.
bullets.treat: Hydrate and check hearing, then stop for a rising creatinine.
bullets.trap: Do not give it to a dry patient.

source.recommendation: Cisplatin is ototoxic and nephrotoxic. Chloride diuresis reduces the renal injury.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Protect the kidney with chloride diuresis.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A tuberculosis drug turns body fluids orange and makes other drugs fail, including contraception.
bottom: It induces the enzymes that clear other drugs.

bullets.clue: The orange color is harmless. The lost drug effect is not.
bullets.treat: Warn about contraception, then do not stop the drug for orange urine.
bullets.trap: Do not call orange tears liver failure.

source.recommendation: Rifampin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase, colors fluids orange, and induces CYP enzymes.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. It induces the enzymes that clear other drugs.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A tuberculosis drug injures the liver and causes numbness unless a vitamin is given.
bottom: Give vitamin B6 with it.

bullets.clue: The vitamin prevents the neuropathy. It does not cancel the liver risk.
bullets.treat: Give B6, then stop the drug for hepatitis.
bullets.trap: Do not skip B6 in a patient at risk of neuropathy.

source.recommendation: Isoniazid causes vitamin B6 deficiency neuropathy and hepatitis. Pyridoxine is coadministered.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Give vitamin B6 with it.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A tuberculosis drug causes trouble telling red from green.
bottom: Stop it if color vision changes.

bullets.clue: The optic nerve is the target.
bullets.treat: Check vision, then do not push the dose through a color change.
bullets.trap: Do not blame the eyes on the orange-fluid drug.

source.recommendation: Ethambutol causes optic neuritis with red-green color loss.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Stop it if color vision changes.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A tuberculosis drug raises uric acid.
bottom: The gout is from this drug, not from the orange-fluid drug.

bullets.clue: Urate rises because excretion falls.
bullets.treat: Treat the joint if it flares, then do not stop the whole regimen for a mild urate rise alone.
bullets.trap: Do not add a xanthine-oxidase blocker without checking the other drugs.

source.recommendation: Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricemia.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The gout is from this drug, not from the orange-fluid drug.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: An antifungal punches holes by binding the fungal membrane sterol. The kidney wastes potassium and magnesium.
bottom: The sterol is ergosterol.

bullets.clue: Humans use cholesterol, but the drug is still kidney-toxic.
bullets.treat: Hydrate and replace the salts, then a lipid form lowers the kidney hit.
bullets.trap: Do not use it for a mild skin fungus.

source.recommendation: Amphotericin binds ergosterol. Nephrotoxicity wastes potassium and magnesium.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The sterol is ergosterol.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: An antifungal blocks synthesis of the fungal membrane sterol and also blocks human drug-clearing enzymes.
bottom: Synthesis block vs a hole punch.

bullets.clue: The hole-punch drug binds the sterol. This class blocks making it.
bullets.treat: Watch drug levels of medicines cleared by those enzymes, then do not stack them blindly.
bullets.trap: Do not treat every antifungal as kidney-safe.

source.recommendation: Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis and CYP enzymes. Amphotericin binds ergosterol directly.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Synthesis block vs a hole punch.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: An antiviral must be activated by a viral enzyme. A resistant virus lacks that enzyme.
bottom: The virus supplies the first phosphorylation.

bullets.clue: If the enzyme is gone, the drug never turns on.
bullets.treat: Use a drug that does not need that enzyme when resistance is this type, then do not raise the dose.
bullets.trap: Do not expect the drug to work in a virus with no thymidine kinase.

source.recommendation: Acyclovir requires viral thymidine kinase for its first phosphorylation.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The virus supplies the first phosphorylation.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A flu drug blocks the enzyme that lets new virus leave the cell. It works only if started early.
bottom: Start within the first two days of symptoms.

bullets.clue: Later doses do not rewind replication that already happened.
bullets.treat: Give it early for severe risk, then do not use it as a substitute for the vaccine.
bullets.trap: Do not start it on day 6 and expect a cure.

source.recommendation: Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor and is most useful within 48 hours of symptom onset.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Start within the first two days of symptoms.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A gram-positive drug binds a cell-wall peptide. Infused too fast, it reddens the patient without a true allergy.
bottom: Slow the infusion.

bullets.clue: The red flush is histamine, not an IgE allergy.
bullets.treat: Slow the rate, then do not write a lifelong allergy for a flush.
bullets.trap: Do not treat ordinary flushing with drug desensitization.

source.recommendation: Vancomycin binds D-ala-D-ala. Rapid infusion causes red-man syndrome from histamine, not IgE.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Slow the infusion.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: An antibiotic binds the 30S subunit, needs oxygen to enter, and injures ear and kidney.
bottom: It fails against anaerobes.

bullets.clue: Oxygen-dependent uptake is why abscesses resist it.
bullets.treat: Dose by level and kidney function, then do not use it alone in a closed abscess.
bullets.trap: Do not pair it with a drug that has the same ear and kidney hit unless you must.

source.recommendation: Aminoglycosides bind 30S, require oxygen for uptake, and are ototoxic and nephrotoxic.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. It fails against anaerobes.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: An antibiotic binds the 50S subunit, prolongs the QT interval, and raises levels of other drugs.
bottom: The heart rhythm is the trap.

bullets.clue: The enzyme block raises statin and other drug levels.
bullets.treat: Check the other medicines, then do not use it for a trivial cough.
bullets.trap: Do not ignore a long QT.

source.recommendation: Macrolides bind 50S, prolong QT, and inhibit CYP3A4.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The heart rhythm is the trap.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: An antibiotic stains new teeth and can injure fetal bone. It also fails with milk.
bottom: Do not use it in pregnancy or young children.

bullets.clue: Calcium in milk binds the drug.
bullets.treat: Pick another agent, then do not give it with dairy.
bullets.trap: Do not use it for a child under 8.

source.recommendation: Tetracyclines bind 30S, discolor teeth, and are avoided in pregnancy and children under 8.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Do not use it in pregnancy or young children.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: An antibiotic can rupture a tendon and is avoided when a better drug exists for a simple urine infection.
bottom: The tendon is the signature injury.

bullets.clue: Cartilage harm is why children are usually spared.
bullets.treat: Stop at the first tendon pain, then choose a different class.
bullets.trap: Do not use it as the first pill for simple cystitis.

source.recommendation: Fluoroquinolones cause tendinopathy and are not first-line for uncomplicated cystitis.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The tendon is the signature injury.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: An anaerobic drug causes severe vomiting with alcohol.
bottom: Warn the patient before the first dose.

bullets.clue: The reaction is like the alcohol-sensitizing drug.
bullets.treat: Avoid alcohol during the course and for a short time after, then do not call the vomiting an allergy to the drug.
bullets.trap: Do not prescribe it with a drink the same night.

source.recommendation: Metronidazole has a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol and covers anaerobes below the diaphragm.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Warn the patient before the first dose.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: Two drugs block two steps of the same folate path. Together they raise potassium.
bottom: The potassium rise is the trap in older adults.

bullets.clue: Each drug alone is weaker. Together they stop bacterial folate.
bullets.treat: Watch potassium, then do not use it for a simple throat infection.
bullets.trap: Do not ignore a creatinine rise on this pair.

source.recommendation: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole blocks two folate steps and can cause hyperkalemia.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The potassium rise is the trap in older adults.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A farmer is wet with saliva and has tiny pupils. The enzyme that clears acetylcholine is glued shut.
bottom: Atropine first, then the regenerator.

bullets.clue: Atropine dries the secretions. The regenerator can restore the enzyme if given early.
bullets.treat: Atropine until secretions dry, then the oxime, and do not delay atropine for the oxime.
bullets.trap: Do not give the regenerator and skip atropine.

source.recommendation: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Atropine is immediate. Pralidoxime regenerates the enzyme if early.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Atropine first, then the regenerator.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A fire victim has a normal pulse oximeter, lactic acidosis, and bitter-almond breath. The blocked step is complex IV.
bottom: Give the vitamin B12 antidote.

bullets.clue: The oximeter cannot see this poisoning.
bullets.treat: Hydroxocobalamin now, then oxygen. Do not wait for a lab.
bullets.trap: Do not treat this as simple smoke inhalation.

source.recommendation: Cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, complex IV. Hydroxocobalamin is the antidote.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Give the vitamin B12 antidote.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: Chocolate-brown blood that does not pink up with oxygen. A dye can reverse it, except when the sugar enzyme is missing.
bottom: The iron is stuck in the wrong charge.

bullets.clue: The dye is the antidote in patients who can make NADPH.
bullets.treat: Give the dye if the level is high and the enzyme is intact, then do not give it in that enzyme deficiency.
bullets.trap: Do not keep raising the oxygen and stop there.

source.recommendation: Methemoglobinemia is treated with methylene blue, which is avoided in G6PD deficiency.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The iron is stuck in the wrong charge.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: Headache in a family with a bad heater. The oxygen curve shifts toward holding oxygen tighter. The oximeter reads normal.
bottom: The curve shifts left.

bullets.clue: The poison binds hemoglobin far more tightly than oxygen.
bullets.treat: Give 100 percent oxygen, then consider a pressure chamber for severe cases.
bullets.trap: Do not trust the finger probe.

source.recommendation: Carbon monoxide shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve left and is invisible to standard pulse oximetry.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The curve shifts left.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A pain drug is safe until glutathione runs out. Then a toxic metabolite appears.
bottom: The antidote refills glutathione.

bullets.clue: The toxic metabolite is what injures the liver, hours later.
bullets.treat: Give the antidote from the timed level, then do not wait for the liver enzymes to rise.
bullets.trap: Do not discharge a large ingestion because the patient feels well.

source.recommendation: Acetaminophen depletes glutathione and forms NAPQI. N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The antidote refills glutathione.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A child with a viral illness is given aspirin and then vomits and becomes sleepy with liver failure.
bottom: Do not give aspirin to children with a viral illness.

bullets.clue: The liver and the brain are both hit.
bullets.treat: Support the liver failure, then never use aspirin for routine childhood fever.
bullets.trap: Do not substitute aspirin for a viral fever.

source.recommendation: Aspirin in children with viral illness is associated with Reye syndrome: liver failure and encephalopathy.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Do not give aspirin to children with a viral illness.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A paralytic used for intubation raises potassium dangerously in a patient with burns or a denervating injury.
bottom: Pick a different paralytic.

bullets.clue: The drug opens receptors and lets potassium pour out. Injured muscle has too many receptors.
bullets.treat: Use a nondepolarizing drug, then do not use this one in burns, crush, or denervation.
bullets.trap: Do not reverse this drug with the cholinesterase inhibitor.

source.recommendation: Succinylcholine causes life-threatening hyperkalemia in burns and denervation. It is not reversed by neostigmine.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Pick a different paralytic.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A sodium-channel blocker binds more when the heart is beating fast.
bottom: Use dependence.

bullets.clue: Open and inactive channels are the ones the drug prefers.
bullets.treat: The fast rate is when the drug works best, then a normal rate lets it unbind.
bullets.trap: Do not expect the same block on a slow heart.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: class I antiarrhythmics
source.recommendation: Class I sodium-channel blockers show use dependence: more binding at faster heart rates.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Use dependence.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A potassium-channel blocker prolongs the QT interval and can cause a twisting ventricular rhythm.
bottom: Keep the potassium and magnesium normal.

bullets.clue: A long QT is the setup for the twist.
bullets.treat: Stop the offending drug and replace magnesium, then do not add a second QT drug.
bullets.trap: Do not treat the twist with another QT-prolonging agent.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: class III and torsades
source.recommendation: Class III potassium-channel block prolongs QT and can precipitate torsades de pointes.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Keep the potassium and magnesium normal.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A six-second push stops a sudden narrow fast rhythm. Theophylline blocks the same receptor.
bottom: The push is adenosine.

bullets.clue: The half-life is seconds. Theophylline and caffeine antagonize it.
bullets.treat: Push it fast with a flush, then do not use it for an irregular wide rhythm that might be fibrillation.
bullets.trap: Do not give it for atrial fibrillation with a wide complex from an extra pathway.

source.recommendation: Adenosine terminates AV-node-dependent supraventricular tachycardia. Methylxanthines block its receptor.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The push is adenosine.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A chest-pain drug dilates veins more than arteries, so preload falls. A holiday from it can cause a rebound headache.
bottom: Veins first.

bullets.clue: Less preload means less wall stress and less oxygen need.
bullets.treat: Give a nitrate-free interval, then do not combine it with a potency drug for erection.
bullets.trap: Do not stack it with sildenafil.

source.recommendation: Nitrates are venodilators that lower preload. They are contraindicated with PDE-5 inhibitors.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Veins first.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A direct arterial dilator causes a fast heart rate and a lupus-like picture.
bottom: The reflex rate is expected.

bullets.clue: A beta blocker is often paired so the heart does not race.
bullets.treat: Add the rate control, then do not use this drug alone in a patient with coronary disease.
bullets.trap: Do not ignore the tachycardia.

source.recommendation: Hydralazine dilates arterioles, causes reflex tachycardia, and can cause drug-induced lupus.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The reflex rate is expected.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A drip for severe pressure can release cyanide if the infusion runs too long.
bottom: The limit is time and dose.

bullets.clue: The body uses thiosulfate to clear the cyanide. That pool runs out.
bullets.treat: Keep the infusion short, then switch to another agent.
bullets.trap: Do not run it for days.

source.recommendation: Prolonged nitroprusside infusion can cause cyanide toxicity.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The limit is time and dose.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A potassium-sparing diuretic grows breast tissue in men.
bottom: The hormone-like effect is the clue.

bullets.clue: A cousin drug spares potassium with less of that effect.
bullets.treat: Switch if the breast tissue is the problem, then keep watching potassium.
bullets.trap: Do not add potassium supplements on top.

source.recommendation: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone and can cause gynecomastia. Eplerenone is less likely to.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The hormone-like effect is the clue.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: An osmotic diuretic is used for brain swelling. It is dangerous when the lungs are already wet.
bottom: Do not give it in heart failure.

bullets.clue: The sugar stays outside cells and pulls water into the vessels.
bullets.treat: Use it for high pressure in the skull when the lungs are dry, then do not use it as a daily water pill.
bullets.trap: Do not give it to a patient in pulmonary edema.

source.recommendation: Mannitol pulls water into the vascular space and is contraindicated in pulmonary edema.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Do not give it in heart failure.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A diuretic used for altitude sickness causes a metabolic acidosis on purpose.
bottom: Bicarbonate is lost in the urine.

bullets.clue: The acidosis raises ventilation, which helps at altitude.
bullets.treat: Use it for prevention of altitude illness, then do not use it as a strong volume diuretic.
bullets.trap: Do not expect it to waste potassium like a loop.

source.recommendation: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase, wastes bicarbonate, and is used to prevent altitude sickness.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Bicarbonate is lost in the urine.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A gout drug blocks penicillin excretion and is not used during an acute flare.
bottom: It raises penicillin levels and lowers urate over time.

bullets.clue: An acute flare needs a different drug. This one can worsen the flare at the start.
bullets.treat: Start it after the flare is quiet, then do not start it on day one of a hot joint.
bullets.trap: Do not use it in an acute attack.

source.recommendation: Probenecid blocks penicillin secretion and is a uricosuric. It is not treatment for an acute gout flare.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. It raises penicillin levels and lowers urate over time.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A gout drug blocks the enzyme that makes uric acid. It is also not the drug for the first day of a hot joint.
bottom: Lower the urate between attacks.

bullets.clue: Starting it during a flare can prolong the pain.
bullets.treat: Treat the flare first, then start this drug with cover.
bullets.trap: Do not start it alone on day one of the flare.

source.recommendation: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase. It is started after a flare settles, not as the sole acute treatment.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Lower the urate between attacks.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A gout drug stops white cells by freezing their skeletons. Diarrhea is the limit.
bottom: The skeleton is the microtubule.

bullets.clue: It does not lower the urate.
bullets.treat: Use a low dose early in the flare, then stop if diarrhea is severe.
bullets.trap: Do not use it as a urate-lowering plan.

source.recommendation: Colchicine inhibits microtubules and neutrophil migration. It does not lower serum urate.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The skeleton is the microtubule.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A pain drug permanently blocks the cyclooxygenase until new enzyme is made. Platelets cannot make new enzyme.
bottom: The platelet effect lasts the life of the platelet.

bullets.clue: Other tissues can make new enzyme. Platelets cannot.
bullets.treat: The antiplatelet effect is days, then do not expect it to wear off in one night.
bullets.trap: Do not hold one dose and operate the same day for bleeding risk.

source.recommendation: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX. Platelets cannot resynthesize it, so the effect lasts their lifespan.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The platelet effect lasts the life of the platelet.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A pain drug that spares the stomach enzyme can raise clot risk.
bottom: The vessel enzyme makes the anti-clot prostaglandin.

bullets.clue: Blocking it removes a brake on platelets.
bullets.treat: Avoid it in patients with high clot risk, then do not call it heart-safe.
bullets.trap: Do not use it as a safer arthritis drug after a heart attack.

source.recommendation: COX-2 inhibitors reduce gastroprotection concerns but increase thrombotic risk by lowering prostacyclin.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The vessel enzyme makes the anti-clot prostaglandin.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A steroid raises the neutrophil count on the smear without meaning a new infection.
bottom: The cells leave the vessel wall and show up in the blood.

bullets.clue: The count rises. The cells are not better at killing.
bullets.treat: Do not chase the number with antibiotics, then look at the patient.
bullets.trap: Do not treat demargination as sepsis.

source.recommendation: Glucocorticoids demarginate neutrophils, raising the count without a new infection.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The cells leave the vessel wall and show up in the blood.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A patient with a pheo is given a beta blocker first. The pressure rises.
bottom: Block alpha first, then beta.

bullets.clue: Beta block alone leaves alpha constriction unopposed.
bullets.treat: Phenoxybenzamine first, then a beta blocker if the heart is fast.
bullets.trap: Do not lead with the beta blocker.

source.recommendation: Pheochromocytoma requires alpha blockade before beta blockade to avoid unopposed alpha vasoconstriction.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Block alpha first, then beta.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A partial activator can block a full activator at the same receptor.
bottom: It occupies the receptor and produces less effect.

bullets.clue: That is why it can precipitate withdrawal in a dependent patient.
bullets.treat: Use it when that mixed effect is the goal, then do not stack it on a full agonist unknowingly.
bullets.trap: Do not call it a pure blocker.

source.recommendation: A partial agonist has lower efficacy and can antagonize a full agonist at the same receptor.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. It occupies the receptor and produces less effect.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A tuberculosis drug makes birth-control pills fail.
bottom: Enzyme induction clears the hormone.

bullets.clue: The patient can become pregnant while taking the pills perfectly.
bullets.treat: Use a second method, then do not rely on the pill alone.
bullets.trap: Do not wait for a missed period to mention it.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: rifampin and contraception
source.recommendation: Rifampin induces CYP3A4 and reduces the effectiveness of combined oral contraceptives.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Enzyme induction clears the hormone.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A weak acid is trapped in alkaline urine. A weak base is trapped in acid urine.
bottom: Ionized drug does not cross back.

bullets.clue: Alkaline urine holds aspirin. Acid urine holds a base such as quinidine.
bullets.treat: Alkalinize for a serious aspirin overdose, then do not acidify urine as a routine trick.
bullets.trap: Do not alkalinize every overdose.

source.recommendation: Ionized species are trapped. Alkaline urine increases salicylate excretion.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Ionized drug does not cross back.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A drug is swallowed and most of it is cleared by the liver before it reaches the body.
bottom: That loss is the first pass.

bullets.clue: A high first-pass drug needs a much larger oral dose than an intravenous dose.
bullets.treat: Choose the route for the dose you intend, then do not convert one-to-one.
bullets.trap: Do not give the intravenous dose by mouth and expect the same level.

source.recommendation: First-pass hepatic extraction means oral and intravenous doses are not interchangeable.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. That loss is the first pass.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: Which drugs have a narrow gap between the helpful dose and the dangerous dose?
bottom: Warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin, and theophylline.

bullets.clue: A small dose change moves the level a lot once enzymes are full.
bullets.treat: Check levels and kidneys, then do not refill a doubled dose.
bullets.trap: Do not treat these like a wide-margin pain drug.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: narrow therapeutic index
source.recommendation: Narrow-index drugs include warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin, and theophylline.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin, and theophylline.

front: Swelling from high pressure in the capillaries vs swelling from low protein in the blood.
bottom: Pressure push vs protein pull.

bullets.clue: Heart failure raises the push. Nephrotic syndrome and cirrhosis lower the pull.
bullets.treat: Treat the pressure or the protein, then do not give albumin for ordinary heart failure.
bullets.trap: Do not use one diuretic plan for every edema.

source.recommendation: Edema is high capillary hydrostatic pressure or low plasma oncotic pressure, among other forces.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Pressure push vs protein pull.

front: A stiff lung has low compliance. A lung that has lost recoil has high compliance.
bottom: Fibrosis vs emphysema.

bullets.clue: Fibrosis is hard to fill. Emphysema is easy to fill and hard to empty.
bullets.treat: Name the curve, then treat the disease, not the number alone.
bullets.trap: Do not say both lungs are stiff.

source.recommendation: Pulmonary fibrosis lowers compliance. Emphysema raises compliance and destroys elastic recoil.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Fibrosis vs emphysema.

front: The ratio of the one-second volume to the full volume is under 0.70. A different patient has a small full volume and a normal ratio.
bottom: Obstruction vs restriction.

bullets.clue: A low ratio is obstruction. A small volume with a preserved ratio is restriction.
bullets.treat: Use the ratio first, then the full volume.
bullets.trap: Do not call every low volume asthma.

source.recommendation: FEV1/FVC under 0.70 indicates obstruction. Restriction lowers volumes with a normal or high ratio.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Obstruction vs restriction.

front: Oxygen is low and the gap between alveolar and arterial oxygen is wide. A different patient has low oxygen and a normal gap.
bottom: Lung problem vs not enough breathing.

bullets.clue: A wide gap means the lung is not transferring. A normal gap means the patient is not ventilating.
bullets.treat: Oxygen and find the lung cause for a wide gap, then ventilate the patient with a normal gap.
bullets.trap: Do not give oxygen and skip the gap.

source.recommendation: An elevated A-a gradient means a gas-exchange problem. A normal gradient with hypoxemia means hypoventilation.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Lung problem vs not enough breathing.

front: In a simple metabolic acidosis, what should the carbon dioxide do?
bottom: It should fall by about 1.2 mm Hg for each 1 mEq fall in bicarbonate.

bullets.clue: If it does not fall that far, a second respiratory acidosis is present.
bullets.treat: Calculate the expected value, then look for the second disorder.
bullets.trap: Do not read a low carbon dioxide as a primary lung disease until you do the math.

source.recommendation: Winter formula estimates the compensatory PCO2 in metabolic acidosis: about 1.5 times bicarbonate plus 8.

diagram.alt: Threshold. It should fall by about 1.2 mm Hg for each 1 mEq fall in bicarbonate.

front: Sodium minus chloride minus bicarbonate. The gap is high. A different acidosis has a normal gap.
bottom: Added acid vs lost bicarbonate.

bullets.clue: A high gap means an unmeasured anion. A normal gap often means diarrhea or a tubular leak of bicarbonate.
bullets.treat: Name the gap, then treat the cause.
bullets.trap: Do not give bicarbonate to every acidosis.

source.recommendation: Anion gap is sodium minus (chloride + bicarbonate). A high gap means unmeasured anions.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Added acid vs lost bicarbonate.

front: A measured osmolality is much higher than the calculated one. The patient drank a toxic alcohol.
bottom: The gap is the unmeasured osmoles.

bullets.clue: Methanol and ethylene glycol raise the gap and later the acid gap.
bullets.treat: Fomepizole, then dialysis if severe. Do not wait for the acid if the osmolar gap and the story are clear.
bullets.trap: Do not treat this as ordinary drunkenness.

source.recommendation: An osmolar gap with anion-gap acidosis suggests methanol or ethylene glycol. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The gap is the unmeasured osmoles.

front: Early aspirin overdose makes the patient breathe fast before the acid builds.
bottom: Respiratory alkalosis first, then anion-gap acidosis.

bullets.clue: The drive to breathe is stimulated early. The acid comes later.
bullets.treat: Alkalinize the urine for severe cases, then do not be reassured by a high pH at hour two.
bullets.trap: Do not call the fast breathing anxiety.

source.recommendation: Salicylate poisoning causes an early respiratory alkalosis and a later anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Respiratory alkalosis first, then anion-gap acidosis.

front: Vomiting loses acid and leaves an alkalosis. A diuretic that empties volume does the same by a different route.
bottom: Lost stomach acid vs a contracted volume.

bullets.clue: Both raise bicarbonate. The urine chloride helps separate a recent vomit from a maintained contraction.
bullets.treat: Replace volume and potassium, then stop the offending diuretic.
bullets.trap: Do not give more acid blindly.

source.recommendation: Vomiting and contraction alkalosis both raise bicarbonate. Urine chloride helps separate them.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Lost stomach acid vs a contracted volume.

front: A child spills glucose, amino acids, and phosphate. Bicarbonate is wasted until the plasma level is low, and then the urine can acidify.
bottom: The proximal tubule is leaking.

bullets.clue: Once plasma bicarbonate is low enough, the distal tubule can still acidify.
bullets.treat: Replace bicarbonate and phosphate, then look for a cause such as a drug.
bullets.trap: Do not call this the distal defect that cannot acidify at all.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: proximal renal tubular acidosis
source.recommendation: Type 2 renal tubular acidosis is proximal bicarbonate wasting and can be part of Fanconi syndrome.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The proximal tubule is leaking.

front: Which substance's clearance equals glomerular filtration, and which equals renal plasma flow?
bottom: Inulin vs PAH.

bullets.clue: Inulin is filtered and not touched. PAH is filtered and fully secreted at low levels.
bullets.treat: Use inulin for filtration and PAH for flow, then do not use creatinine as a perfect inulin.
bullets.trap: Do not swap them.

source.recommendation: Inulin clearance estimates GFR. PAH clearance at low concentration estimates renal plasma flow.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Inulin vs PAH.

front: A hormone from the atria dilates the incoming kidney arteriole and dumps sodium. Aldosterone does the opposite on sodium.
bottom: Heart hormone vs adrenal hormone.

bullets.clue: Stretch releases the heart hormone. Volume depletion releases the adrenal hormone.
bullets.treat: A high heart-hormone level supports a stretched heart, then do not treat the hormone as the disease.
bullets.trap: Do not give salt for a high level.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: ANP vs aldosterone
source.recommendation: ANP causes natriuresis and afferent dilation. Aldosterone retains sodium and wastes potassium.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Heart hormone vs adrenal hormone.

front: A hormone inserts water channels in the collecting duct. Its cousin causes milk let-down and uterine contraction.
bottom: Water channel vs contraction.

bullets.clue: The water hormone uses the V2 receptor. The contraction hormone uses a different receptor.
bullets.treat: Replace the water hormone when it is missing, then do not use the contraction drug for diabetes insipidus.
bullets.trap: Do not swap them.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: ADH vs oxytocin
source.recommendation: ADH inserts aquaporin-2 via V2 receptors. Oxytocin causes uterine contraction and milk ejection.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Water channel vs contraction.

front: A pituitary hormone is under constant brake from dopamine. Cutting the stalk raises it and lowers the others.
bottom: Dopamine is the brake.

bullets.clue: Stalk section removes the brake on this hormone and removes the drive for the others.
bullets.treat: A mildly high level can be stalk effect, then a very high level is a tumor of that cell.
bullets.trap: Do not operate every mild elevation.

source.recommendation: Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin. Stalk effect raises prolactin mildly and lowers other pituitary hormones.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Dopamine is the brake.

front: Which hormone maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over?
bottom: The pregnancy hormone from the trophoblast.

bullets.clue: It appears in urine early and is the test.
bullets.treat: A falling level in early pregnancy needs follow-up, then do not call a single low value a miscarriage without the trend.
bullets.trap: Do not use it to date a pregnancy.

source.recommendation: hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The pregnancy hormone from the trophoblast.

front: A sustained rise of one ovarian hormone triggers the surge that releases the egg. The other hormone raises the morning temperature after ovulation.
bottom: Surge trigger vs temperature.

bullets.clue: The surge trigger is the rising ovarian hormone at midcycle. The temperature hormone comes from the corpus luteum.
bullets.treat: Name which hormone, then do not use temperature to time the surge.
bullets.trap: Do not swap them.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: estrogen vs progesterone
source.recommendation: Rising estradiol triggers the LH surge. Progesterone from the corpus luteum raises basal temperature.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Surge trigger vs temperature.

front: One testicular cell feeds the sperm and makes the hormone that slows FSH. The other cell makes testosterone under LH.
bottom: Nurse cell vs hormone cell.

bullets.clue: The nurse cell makes inhibin. The hormone cell makes testosterone.
bullets.treat: FSH drives the nurse cell, then LH drives the hormone cell.
bullets.trap: Do not say FSH makes testosterone.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: Sertoli vs Leydig
source.recommendation: Sertoli cells support spermatogenesis and secrete inhibin. Leydig cells make testosterone under LH.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Nurse cell vs hormone cell.

front: A gene on the Y chromosome makes the gonad a testis. Without it, the gonad becomes an ovary.
bottom: That gene starts the testis.

bullets.clue: The testis then makes two signals that finish the male tract.
bullets.treat: No gene means the ovarian path, then do not look for the gene on the X.
bullets.trap: Do not say the default embryo is male.

source.recommendation: SRY on the Y chromosome directs the bipotential gonad to become a testis. The default path is ovarian.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. That gene starts the testis.

front: The testis makes a hormone that removes the female internal ducts, and a different hormone that keeps the male internal ducts.
bottom: Removal signal vs keeping signal.

bullets.clue: The removal signal is from the nurse cell. Testosterone keeps the male duct.
bullets.treat: Name both, then the external genitals need the more potent androgen.
bullets.trap: Do not say testosterone removes the female ducts.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: Mullerian inhibiting substance
source.recommendation: Sertoli cells secrete Mullerian inhibiting substance. Testosterone stabilizes the Wolffian ducts.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Removal signal vs keeping signal.

front: A baby looks female outside and has no uterus. Testosterone is high, and the receptor does not work.
bottom: The receptor is deaf.

bullets.clue: The outside never saw the androgen. The female ducts were still removed.
bullets.treat: Raise the child with the anatomy she has, then do not start testosterone to grow a uterus.
bullets.trap: Do not search for a uterus that the removal signal already erased.

source.recommendation: Complete androgen insensitivity: female external phenotype, blind vagina, no uterus, and testes.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The receptor is deaf.

front: A baby has ambiguous genitals. Testosterone is present, but the stronger androgen that finishes the outside is not being made.
bottom: The converting enzyme is missing.

bullets.clue: The internal male ducts, which need testosterone itself, are present.
bullets.treat: Raise with support, then do not call this a missing testis.
bullets.trap: Do not give the stronger androgen without a specialist plan.

source.recommendation: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency: testosterone is present, DHT is not, so external genitalia are ambiguous.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The converting enzyme is missing.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: A tall teen has small firm testes and no sperm. The karyotype has an extra X.
bottom: 47,XXY.

bullets.clue: The extra X silences the testes.
bullets.treat: Replace testosterone at puberty, then do not promise fertility.
bullets.trap: Do not call this the single-X syndrome. That one is short, not tall.

source.recommendation: Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY: tall stature, small testes, azoospermia, and hypogonadism.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. 47,XXY.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: A boy has a long face, large ears, and a large jaw. The repeat is CGG and it sits on the X.
bottom: The repeat silences the gene.

bullets.clue: More repeats in later generations means earlier, worse disease.
bullets.treat: Support development, then test the mother who may carry a premutation.
bullets.trap: Do not call this the trinucleotide disease of the movement disorder.

source.recommendation: Fragile X is a CGG repeat in FMR1 with anticipation. It is the common inherited cause of intellectual disability.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The repeat silences the gene.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: A movement disease appears earlier in each generation. The repeat is CAG.
bottom: More repeats, earlier disease.

bullets.clue: The protein gains a toxic function. It is not a missing enzyme.
bullets.treat: Counsel about anticipation, then do not promise a diet that removes the repeat.
bullets.trap: Do not call this a recessive enzyme block.

source.recommendation: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant CAG repeat with anticipation and a toxic gain of function.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. More repeats, earlier disease.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: Grip cannot release, and cataracts appear. The repeat is CTG and it worsens in the next generation.
bottom: Cannot let go.

bullets.clue: The muscle disease and the anticipation travel together.
bullets.treat: Support the weakness, then watch the heart rhythm.
bullets.trap: Do not call this ordinary muscle soreness.

source.recommendation: Myotonic dystrophy is a CTG repeat: myotonia, cataracts, and anticipation.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Cannot let go.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: A disease passes from a mother to all of her children and from none of the fathers.
bottom: The DNA is in the mitochondria.

bullets.clue: Fathers do not pass mitochondria in any meaningful amount.
bullets.treat: Draw the pedigree, then do not call it X-linked. Fathers with X-linked disease pass it to daughters.
bullets.trap: Do not expect an affected father to have affected children.

source.recommendation: Mitochondrial diseases are transmitted by the mother to all children. Affected fathers do not transmit them.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The DNA is in the mitochondria.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: An extra chromosome 21 from a fusion of two long arms. The count of chromosomes looks like 45 in a carrier.
bottom: A fusion, not a free extra chromosome.

bullets.clue: A carrier can pass an unbalanced set.
bullets.treat: Counsel the carrier parent, then do not reassure from a normal total in the parent.
bullets.trap: Do not stop at the child's karyotype.

source.recommendation: A Robertsonian translocation can cause familial Down syndrome. A balanced carrier has 45 chromosomes.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. A fusion, not a free extra chromosome.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: Rocker-bottom feet, clenched fists, and a low AFP. The extra chromosome is 18. A different infant has clefts and extra fingers and an extra 13.

bullets.clue: Both are severe. The hand and foot point at 18. The cleft and extra fingers point at 13.
bullets.treat: Support the infant, then confirm with a karyotype.
bullets.trap: Do not mix the chromosome numbers.

source.recommendation: Trisomy 18: clenched fists and rocker-bottom feet. Trisomy 13: cleft, polydactyly, and holoprosencephaly.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. 18 vs 13.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: A high-pitched cry, a small head, and a missing piece of the short arm of chromosome 5.
bottom: The cry is the clue.

bullets.clue: The deletion is 5p.
bullets.treat: Support development, then do not call every small head this syndrome.
bullets.trap: Do not wait for the cry to disappear before testing.

source.recommendation: Cri-du-chat is a 5p deletion: high-pitched cry, microcephaly, and intellectual disability.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The cry is the clue.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: A very social child, supravalvular aortic narrowing, and high calcium. Elastin is the gene.
bottom: Elastin.

bullets.clue: The personality and the aortic narrowing travel together.
bullets.treat: Image the aorta, then watch the calcium.
bullets.trap: Do not call this the downward-lens disease.

source.recommendation: Williams syndrome is an elastin deletion: supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcemia, and a social personality.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Elastin.

front: Folate before conception lowers the chance of an open neural tube. A high AFP in the amniotic fluid means the tube is open. A low AFP suggests an extra 21.
bottom: High AFP vs low AFP.

bullets.clue: Open tube leaks AFP. An extra 21 lowers it.
bullets.treat: Folate before pregnancy, then interpret AFP with the ultrasound.
bullets.trap: Do not start folate after the tube has closed and expect it to fix the defect.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: neural tube and AFP
source.recommendation: Periconceptional folate lowers neural-tube-defect risk. High AFP suggests an open defect. Low AFP suggests trisomy 21.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. High AFP vs low AFP.

front: A newborn has a double bubble and polyhydramnios. The recanalization of the gut failed. A different newborn has a covered midline abdominal sac.
bottom: Failed recanalization vs a failed return of the gut.

bullets.clue: The double bubble is a closed duodenum. The covered sac is a different wall defect.
bullets.treat: Surgery for both, then they are not the same operation.
bullets.trap: Do not call every abdominal-wall defect a closed duodenum.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: duodenal atresia vs omphalocele
source.recommendation: Duodenal atresia shows a double bubble and polyhydramnios. Omphalocele is a covered midline wall defect.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Failed recanalization vs a failed return of the gut.

front: A painless maroon stool in a toddler. The remnant is a true diverticulum on the anti-mesenteric side of the ileum.
bottom: Two feet from the valve, two inches, two tissues.

bullets.clue: It can contain stomach tissue that bleeds.
bullets.treat: Scan if the story fits, then do not call every painless bleed a fissure.
bullets.trap: Do not ignore a large painless bleed.

source.recommendation: Meckel diverticulum is a vitelline-duct remnant that can contain gastric mucosa and bleed.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Two feet from the valve, two inches, two tissues.

front: A newborn chokes on the first feed. Air fills the stomach, and the esophagus ends in a blind pouch.
bottom: The pouch and the fistula travel together.

bullets.clue: Air in the stomach means the lower fistula reaches the airway.
bullets.treat: Surgery, then do not keep feeding.
bullets.trap: Do not call this simple reflux.

source.recommendation: The common tracheoesophageal anomaly is esophageal atresia with a distal fistula. Choking on feeds is the clue.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The pouch and the fistula travel together.

front: Too little fluid: a crushed face and lungs that never grew. Too much fluid: a gut that cannot swallow.
bottom: Low fluid vs high fluid.

bullets.clue: Low fluid comes from missing kidneys or a leak. High fluid comes from a swallow block.
bullets.treat: Image the kidneys for low fluid, then image the gut for high fluid.
bullets.trap: Do not treat them as the same ultrasound finding.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: amniotic fluid volume
source.recommendation: Oligohydramnios causes Potter sequence. Polyhydramnios suggests impaired fetal swallowing, such as atresia.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Low fluid vs high fluid.

front: Heart muscle is fed when the aortic valve is closed, not when it is open.
bottom: Flow is in diastole.

bullets.clue: Open aortic valve means the heart is squeezing and compressing the wall vessels.
bullets.treat: A fast rate steals filling time, then that is why rate control helps the ischemic heart.
bullets.trap: Do not say the coronaries fill in systole.

source.recommendation: Coronary perfusion of the left ventricle occurs in diastole.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Flow is in diastole.

front: A third heart sound means a volume overload. A fourth heart sound means a stiff ventricle.
bottom: Volume vs stiffness.

bullets.clue: The third sound is early filling into a full chamber. The fourth is the atrial kick into a stiff chamber.
bullets.treat: Treat the volume or the stiffness, then do not call every extra sound a murmur.
bullets.trap: Do not ignore a new third sound in an adult.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: S3 vs S4
source.recommendation: S3 indicates volume overload. S4 indicates a stiff, noncompliant ventricle.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Volume vs stiffness.

front: A diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap. A different lesion is a holosystolic murmur at the apex into the axilla.
bottom: Narrow valve vs leaky valve.

bullets.clue: The snap is the narrow mitral valve opening. The holosystolic jet is the leak.
bullets.treat: The narrow valve is mechanical. The leak can be ischemic.
bullets.trap: Do not call every apex murmur the narrow valve.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: mitral stenosis vs regurgitation
source.recommendation: Mitral stenosis is a diastolic rumble with an opening snap. Mitral regurgitation is holosystolic into the axilla.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Narrow valve vs leaky valve.

front: A fixed split of the second sound. A different child has a holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border.
bottom: Atrial hole vs ventricular hole.

bullets.clue: Fixed split means the atrial hole. The loud left-sternal murmur means the ventricular hole.
bullets.treat: Both can be watched or closed depending on size, then they are not the same sound.
bullets.trap: Do not call every murmur a ventricular hole.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: ASD vs VSD
source.recommendation: ASD causes fixed splitting of S2. A VSD is a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Atrial hole vs ventricular hole.

front: A murmur gets louder when the patient bears down. Most murmurs get softer.
bottom: The thick septum gets worse when the chamber is smaller.

bullets.clue: Less filling makes the obstruction worse.
bullets.treat: Avoid dehydration and pure dilators, then a beta blocker can help.
bullets.trap: Do not give a nitrate as if this were ordinary chest pain.

source.recommendation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy gets louder with Valsalva because smaller LV volume worsens the obstruction.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The thick septum gets worse when the chamber is smaller.

front: Which murmurs get louder on inspiration?
bottom: The right-sided ones.

bullets.clue: Inspiration pulls more blood into the right heart.
bullets.treat: Use inspiration to place the murmur, then do not call a louder inspiration murmur mitral.
bullets.trap: Do not skip the maneuver.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: respiratory murmur split
source.recommendation: Right-sided murmurs get louder with inspiration. Left-sided murmurs do not.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The right-sided ones.

front: The pacemaker sits at the junction of the big vein and the right atrium. The delay that lets the atrium finish is the next station.
bottom: Sinus node, then the atrioventricular node.

bullets.clue: The delay is the PR interval.
bullets.treat: A long PR is a delay at that station, then a dropped beat is a higher-grade block.
bullets.trap: Do not pace every long PR.

source.recommendation: The SA node sets the rate. The AV node delays conduction so the atrium empties before the ventricle contracts.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Sinus node, then the atrioventricular node.

front: Phase 0 of the ventricular muscle cell is a sodium rush. Phase 2 is the calcium plateau. Phase 3 is potassium leaving.
bottom: Sodium, then calcium, then potassium.

bullets.clue: The plateau is why the heart cannot tetanize.
bullets.treat: Sodium blockers hit phase 0, then calcium blockers hit the node more than this plateau.
bullets.trap: Do not say the whole action potential is one ion.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: cardiac action potential
source.recommendation: Ventricular phase 0 is sodium. Phase 2 is calcium. Phase 3 is potassium efflux.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Sodium, then calcium, then potassium.

front: Pacemaker cells climb to threshold on their own. The current is the funny current.
bottom: They do not need a neighbor to fire.

bullets.clue: Phase 4 is the slow climb.
bullets.treat: A blocker of that climb slows the rate, then a block of the fast sodium current is a different cell.
bullets.trap: Do not treat pacemaker cells as ventricular muscle.

source.recommendation: Pacemaker phase 4 uses the funny current. These cells depolarize spontaneously.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. They do not need a neighbor to fire.

front: An extra pathway from atrium to ventricle shows a short PR and a slurred upstroke. A drug that blocks the node can be dangerous if fibrillation starts.
bottom: The extra path skips the delay.

bullets.clue: Blocking the node sends fibrillation down the extra path.
bullets.treat: Procainamide is the safer acute drug if the path is conducting, then do not push the node blocker.
bullets.trap: Do not give a node blocker for irregular wide fibrillation in this setting.

source.recommendation: Ventricular pre-excitation has a short PR and a delta wave. AV-nodal blockers can accelerate conduction in atrial fibrillation.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The extra path skips the delay.

front: A stroke of the dominant lower frontal lobe. Speech is effortful and the arm is weak. Comprehension is intact.
bottom: The front of the language area.

bullets.clue: Comprehension lives farther back. This lesion is next to the motor face and arm.
bullets.treat: Support the airway of speech, then do not call fluent nonsense this lesion.
bullets.trap: Do not swap it with the temporal lesion.

source.recommendation: Nonfluent aphasia is a dominant frontal lesion: effortful speech, intact comprehension, and nearby arm weakness.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The front of the language area.

front: One pupil is large and the eye is down and out after an aneurysm. A different pupil-sparing palsy is from a small-vessel ischemic nerve in diabetes.
bottom: Compression vs ischemia.

bullets.clue: The parasympathetic fibers ride on the outside, so a squeeze hits the pupil. Ischemia hits the inside and spares it.
bullets.treat: Image a blown pupil, then a spared pupil with a known vascular risk can be watched.
bullets.trap: Do not send a new blown pupil home.

source.recommendation: A compressive third-nerve palsy involves the pupil. An ischemic diabetic palsy often spares it.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Compression vs ischemia.

front: A forehead that cannot wrinkle is a peripheral facial nerve. A forehead that still wrinkles is a central lesion.
bottom: Whole face vs lower face.

bullets.clue: The forehead has backup from both sides of the brain. The lower face does not.
bullets.treat: Protect the eye if the periphery is out, then image the brain if the forehead is spared.
bullets.trap: Do not call a spared forehead Bell palsy.

source.recommendation: Peripheral facial palsy includes the forehead. Central palsy spares the forehead.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Whole face vs lower face.

front: A crescent of blood that crosses suture lines after a slow fall in an older adult. A lens of blood that stops at sutures is the other bleed.
bottom: Bridging veins vs the artery under the temple.

bullets.clue: The crescent is the slow vein. The lens is the artery.
bullets.treat: The lens is the emergency you already know. The crescent can be subacute.
bullets.trap: Do not call every traumatic bleed the artery.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: subdural vs epidural
source.recommendation: Subdural blood is crescentic and crosses sutures. Epidural blood is lens-shaped and stops at sutures.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Bridging veins vs the artery under the temple.

front: A child is tugged by the arm and will not use it. The radial head slipped. Films are normal.
bottom: Reduce it with a turn of the hand.

bullets.clue: The annular ligament is trapped.
bullets.treat: Supinate and flex, then the child uses the arm.
bullets.trap: Do not cast a normal film.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: radial head subluxation
source.recommendation: Nursemaid elbow is annular-ligament subluxation. Reduction is supination and flexion.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Reduce it with a turn of the hand.

front: Morning stiffness of the knuckles and proximal finger joints for over an hour. A different patient has bony knobs of the farthest joints that hurt with use.
bottom: Inflammatory vs wear.

bullets.clue: An hour of stiffness is inflammatory. Use-related farthest joints are wear.
bullets.treat: Start a disease-modifying drug for the inflammatory pattern, then do not use it for simple wear.
bullets.trap: Do not swap the joint patterns.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: rheumatoid vs osteoarthritis pattern
source.recommendation: Rheumatoid arthritis hits MCP and PIP joints with prolonged stiffness. Osteoarthritis hits DIP joints with use.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Inflammatory vs wear.

front: Tense bullae in an older adult. Antibody lines the basement membrane. A different disease has flaccid bullae and a net around each cell.
bottom: Basement membrane vs the glue between cells.

bullets.clue: Tense means the split is under the epidermis. Flaccid means the split is inside it.
bullets.treat: Name the split, then treat the matching disease.
bullets.trap: Do not use one steroid plan without the split.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: pemphigoid vs pemphigus
source.recommendation: Bullous pemphigoid: tense bullae, linear basement-membrane IgG. Pemphigus: flaccid bullae, netlike IgG.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Basement membrane vs the glue between cells.

front: A lower-lip ulcer that can travel. A pearly facial papule that almost never travels.
bottom: The traveling one is squamous. The local one is basal.

bullets.clue: The lower lip is the squamous site. The pearly rolled edge is basal.
bullets.treat: Excise both, then stage only the one that travels.
bullets.trap: Do not freeze a changing dark lesion. That is a third disease.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: squamous vs basal cell
source.recommendation: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma can metastasize. Basal cell carcinoma invades locally and rarely metastasizes.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The traveling one is squamous. The local one is basal.

front: A stress ulcer in the burn patient sits in the duodenum. A stress ulcer in the brain-injury patient sits in the stomach and perforates.
bottom: Duodenum vs stomach.

bullets.clue: Burns point at the duodenum. Head injury points at the stomach.
bullets.treat: Prevent stress ulcers in the critically ill, then do not mix the classic sites.
bullets.trap: Do not call both the same ulcer.

source.recommendation: Curling ulcers are duodenal in burns. Cushing ulcers are gastric in intracranial injury.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Duodenum vs stomach.

front: Right-lower-quadrant pain at the point two-thirds of the way from the navel to the hip bone.
bottom: That point is the appendix.

bullets.clue: Pain starts central and moves there when the lining is irritated.
bullets.treat: Surgical consult if the exam fits, then do not send a peritonitic patient home for a scan tomorrow.
bullets.trap: Do not wait for a fever to believe the exam.

source.recommendation: McBurney point is the surface mark of an inflamed appendix. Migration of pain is the peritoneal sign.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. That point is the appendix.

front: A follicle becomes the corpus luteum after the egg is released. If no pregnancy hormone arrives, it dies and the lining sheds.
bottom: The hormone keeps it. Absence sheds the lining.

bullets.clue: Bleeding is the fall in the hormone, not a high hormone.
bullets.treat: A pregnancy keeps the hormone, then a lost pregnancy loses it.
bullets.trap: Do not call menstrual bleeding an estrogen surge.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: menstrual hormone withdrawal
source.recommendation: Menses follows progesterone withdrawal when the corpus luteum fails and hCG never arrives.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The hormone keeps it. Absence sheds the lining.

front: A cancer at the lung apex drops the eyelid, smalls the pupil, and wastes the hand muscles.
bottom: The chain and the lower brachial plexus are both hit.

bullets.clue: The pupil is small because the sympathetic chain is cut. The hand is the plexus.
bullets.treat: Image the apex, then do not call a small pupil a brain hernia. Herniation blows the pupil.
bullets.trap: Do not miss the apex.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: apical lung tumor
source.recommendation: A Pancoast tumor causes Horner syndrome and hand-muscle wasting by invading the sympathetic chain and brachial plexus.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. The chain and the lower brachial plexus are both hit.

front: A cancer makes the blood too sticky with antibodies in the cold, or too many red cells, or too many platelets. The point is the thickness, not one disease.
bottom: Thickness causes strokes and blurry vision.

bullets.clue: The fix for the emergency is to thin the blood, then treat the cause.
bullets.treat: Remove volume or exchange, then do not give a diuretic and walk away.
bullets.trap: Do not fluid-restrict a patient whose blood is a sludge.

source.recommendation: Hyperviscosity from Waldenstrom, polycythemia, or extreme thrombocytosis is treated by removing the excess cells or protein.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Thickness causes strokes and blurry vision.

task_area: General principles: biology of tissue response to disease
front: A cell shrinks and fragments into tidy bodies without inflammation. A different cell swells and bursts and draws neutrophils.
bottom: Tidy death vs messy death.

bullets.clue: Tidy death is programmed. Messy death spills contents.
bullets.treat: Name which one, then do not treat tidy death as an infection.
bullets.trap: Do not call every dead cell messy death.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: apoptosis vs necrosis
source.recommendation: Apoptosis is ATP-dependent and noninflammatory. Necrosis swells the cell and triggers inflammation.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Tidy death vs messy death.

task_area: General principles: biology of tissue response to disease
front: Apple-green birefringence with Congo red. One protein is a light chain. Another is an acute-phase fragment.
bottom: Light chain vs the acute-phase fragment.

bullets.clue: Light chain means a plasma-cell clone. The acute-phase fragment means a chronic inflammation.
bullets.treat: Find the clone if it is the light chain, then treat the inflammation if it is the other.
bullets.trap: Do not call every amyloid the same disease.

source.recommendation: AL amyloid is immunoglobulin light chain. AA amyloid is serum amyloid A from chronic inflammation.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Light chain vs the acute-phase fragment.

front: Dark urine two days after a sore throat. A different child has dark urine two weeks after skin or throat infection.
bottom: Two days vs two weeks.

bullets.clue: Two days is the immunoglobulin A disease. Two weeks is the post-strep disease.
bullets.treat: Support both, then the post-strep one follows the infection by weeks, not hours.
bullets.trap: Do not treat the two-day disease with penicillin as if the infection were still there.

source.guideline: First Aid-level consensus: IgA nephropathy vs post-strep
source.recommendation: IgA nephropathy is synpharyngitic, within days. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows by 1 to 3 weeks.

diagram.alt: Two-column comparison. Two days vs two weeks.

front: Lung bleed and kidney inflammation. The antibody lines the basement membrane in a smooth ribbon.
bottom: A smooth line of antibody.

bullets.clue: The target is the collagen shared by lung and kidney.
bullets.treat: Treat as a pulmonary-renal emergency, then do not call a lumpy deposit this disease.
bullets.trap: Do not wait for a biopsy if the patient is crashing. Start care.

source.recommendation: Goodpasture syndrome is anti-GBM antibody with linear immunofluorescence in lung and kidney.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. A smooth line of antibody.
